title: Continuous Integration for PHP
learning_outcomes: Explain what continuous integration for php contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: automated tests.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Quality comes from several kinds of evidence: unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, coding standards, and repeatable CI. Tests should assert observable behavior and include important failure and boundary cases. In this lesson, focus on automated tests; then compare it with static analysis. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use continuous integration for php when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Quality comes from several kinds of evidence: unit tests, integration tests, static analysis, coding standards, and repeatable CI. Tests should assert observable behavior and include important failure and boundary cases. For continuous integration for php, begin with automated tests. Also distinguish static analysis; coding-style checks; supported php versions in ci. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: A small PHP example for Continuous Integration for PHP

<?php
$checks = ["unit tests", "integration tests", "static analysis"];
echo implode(", ", $checks) . PHP_EOL;

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Test observable behavior, include boundary cases, and treat static analysis and coverage as evidence rather than proof.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for continuous integration for php from top to bottom. Start by identifying automated tests, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

content.task: Create a second small example for continuous integration for php that demonstrates "automated tests". Before running it, write down the expected result and one boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes a clear use of automated tests.
The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.
At least one edge case is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.
content.expected_output: unit tests, integration tests, static analysis

common_mistakes.why: Boundary inputs and failures can reveal defects that normal examples miss.
common_mistakes.fix: Add empty, invalid, boundary, and failure cases with meaningful assertions.

common_mistakes.why: Tests can become brittle and stop checking real behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer simple unit tests and focused integration tests at actual boundaries.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating coverage as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Executing a line does not guarantee its behavior was asserted.
common_mistakes.fix: Review assertions, relevant branches, edge cases, and regression risk.

summary: Continuous Integration for PHP is one part of the PHP implementation workflow.
Prefer explicit behavior and testable examples over implicit assumptions.
Test observable behavior, include boundary cases, and treat static analysis and coverage as evidence rather than proof.
